articles.title: Flat feet may have helped Neanderthals stay stable while carrying heavy loads
articles.dek: In all likelihood, the Neanderthals had flat feet. But it was not a defect at all.
paragraphs: In all likelihood, the Neanderthals had flat feet. But it was not a defect at all. Instead, it was the consequence of a precise functional strategy to reduce impact stress under heavy loads and maximize stability on mountainous or rough terrain.

This is just one of the findings that emerged from a study— published in the Journal of Human Evolution —that analyzed for the first time the three-dimensional external shape of the entire heel of Neanderthals, comparing it with that of our species, Homo sapiens.

"The human foot is one of the anatomical structures that best demonstrate our complex evolutionary history, and among the bones it is composed of, the heel plays a crucial role: it is the first structure to touch the ground when walking, cushioning the impact and transmitting the forces to push us forward," explains Maria Giovanna Belcastro, professor at the Department of Biological, Geological, and Environmental Sciences of the University of Bologna, who coordinated the study.

"The 3D analysis of the fossil heels of our ancient cousins, the Neanderthals, has therefore allowed us to highlight both an extraordinary biomechanical adaptation to withstand heavy loads and rough terrains, and the impact of modern life and footwear on our feet."

The researchers analyzed and compared the heels of seven individuals of the Homo neanderthalensis species with those of 64 individuals of Homo sapiens, ranging from hunter-gatherers of the Pleistocene to farmers of the Iron Age, up to a postindustrial urban population preserved in the Documented Human Osteological Collection of the Certosa Cemetery of Bologna. To do this, they applied advanced 3D geometric morphometry techniques to digital models obtained with laser scans and computed tomography.

The results show clear and fascinating differences. First, compared to the heels of modern humans, those of Neanderthals were shorter, wider and taller. But one of the most surprising aspects concerns the posture and stability of the Neanderthal foot.

Geometric analysis indicates that Neanderthals' foot posture habitually showed pronation. In addition, the study highlights a lower lateral longitudinal arch in Neanderthals, which offered greater flexibility and mobility in the central part of the foot. In short, Neanderthals had flat feet and used this posture to maximize stability and reduce impact stress under heavy loads.

"The robustness of the heel reflects the overall body structure of Neanderthals, which is characterized by remarkable muscle and bone mass and an extremely intense level of physical activity," confirms Belcastro. "These physical characteristics indicate an adaptation aimed at promoting a greater load-bearing capacity on the back of the foot and high mobility on uneven ground."

Looking instead at our species, the researchers observed that the prehistoric hunter-gatherers of Homo sapiens—who traveled long distances barefoot or with soft footwear—showed heels with characteristics of robustness more similar to those of Neanderthals than those of modern postindustrial populations.

The individuals who have lived in the past centuries have heels that are much weaker, due to a sedentary lifestyle and the habitual use of rigid and closed footwear. This is because the use of shoes with rigid soles tends to limit the inversion and eversion movements of the foot, tightening the ankle: a clear sign of skeletal gracilization due to a drastic reduction in natural biomechanical stimuli.

"The morphology of our skeleton is not only the product of a strict genetic program, but also the consequence of physical stimuli and our daily life habits," explains Belcastro. "The results of this study therefore offer a fundamental contribution to better understand how our ancestors moved in their natural environment and open fascinating prospects for dialogue between evolutionary anthropology and clinical orthopedics."

articles.title: Hundreds of Ice Age rock art engravings discovered hidden in plain sight
articles.dek: Archaeologists have discovered the third-largest assemblage of Ice Age cave art ever found in Mediterranean Iberia in a region thought devoid of cave art, transforming our…
paragraphs: Archaeologists have discovered the third-largest assemblage of Ice Age cave art ever found in Mediterranean Iberia in a region thought devoid of cave art, transforming our knowledge of Paleolithic European art.

Since the 12th century A. D. , people have been visiting the Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia. From 1957 onward, it was widely frequented by visitors, speleologists and treasure hunters, and it was even converted into a tourist attraction in 1993.

Despite this, no art from the Ice Age had ever been discovered there, and it was believed that the cave walls were unsuitable for engraving Paleolithic art. The Iberian Peninsula contains more than 50% of all cave art documented in Upper Paleolithic Europe, but its distribution is uneven, with a high concentration found in the Franco-Cantabrian region (located between modern France and Spain) but only two representations found in the entirety of Catalonia.

"Until now, the Paleolithic rock art identified in northeastern Iberia has been very scarce compared with the abundant record of the neighboring Franco-Cantabrian region," states research co-author Josep Maria Vergès from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA).

This all changed when archaeologists identified 280 Paleolithic motifs in the cave, right under our noses the entire time. This is the highest concentration of Paleolithic parietal representations currently known in Catalonia.

"For more than six decades, thousands of visitors passed directly in front of the engraved surfaces, and in some cases inscribed names and dates over them, without the Paleolithic origin of the figures being recognized," says Vergès.
This discovery means that Cova de la Font Major contains the third-largest Paleolithic cave art assemblage on the Mediterranean side of the Iberian Peninsula.

"Along the Iberian Mediterranean facade, from the Pyrenees to Gibraltar, around 75% of known assemblages contain no more than five zoomorphic figures, and over 90% contain no more than 20," adds co-author Míriam Salas-Altès from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA). "The sheer quantity of art discovered at the Cova de la Font Major is therefore particularly exceptional."

The authors analyzed the rock art and determined that the motifs are different from the art of the neighboring Franco-Cantabrian region, leading them to conclude that this represents a distinct Paleolithic artistic tradition. Their results are published in the journal Antiquity .

These findings demonstrate, for the first time, that northeastern Iberia was home to its own particular artistic customs. The quantity of art could indicate that the region, previously seen as marginal, was densely occupied, transforming our understanding of the Paleolithic in the western Mediterranean.

"Contrary to what was previously thought, northeastern Iberia holds first-rate Paleolithic rock art sites," concludes Salas-Altès. "The Mediterranean art of western Europe is now enriched by a new body of rock art, which allows us to characterize in greater depth a Mediterranean graphic tradition with an identity of its own, distinct from that of the Franco-Cantabrian region."

articles.title: Trust in influencers grows more important in predicting buying intentions over time, analysis finds
articles.dek: A meta-analysis of empirical studies involving more than 31,000 participants has revealed the factors that affect the level of influence of so-called social media…
paragraphs: A meta-analysis of empirical studies involving more than 31,000 participants has revealed the factors that affect the level of influence of so-called social media influencers. Those factors include credibility, expertise, attractiveness and perceived similarity to their followers. They are, the work shows, positively associated with the attitude of consumers toward the brands mentioned or promoted by those influencers and, in turn, their purchasing intentions. Details of the analysis are published in the International Journal of Internet Marketing and Advertising .

The researchers emphasize that a parasocial interaction , the sense of personal connection, is the thing that most deeply affects the relationship between follower and influencer, despite the inevitable asymmetry of the connection. The team also found that all of the factors showed similarly strong relationships with brand attitudes and purchase intentions. This suggests that no single characteristic dominates the effectiveness of influencer marketing. This thus has implications for businesses selecting influencers to help them publicize their products and services.

The analysis also found that credibility has become increasingly important in predicting purchase intentions over time. This perhaps reflects the growing reliance of consumers on trustworthy sources for guidance given the endlessly expanding volume of social media content. This may become an increasingly important part of influencer marketing as artificial intelligence, or AI, becomes more pervasive and consumers seek out genuine content.

articles.title: Carbon dots fluoresce their way through the rainbow as liquids change
articles.dek: Fluorescent materials usually emit a single consistent color. They are typically made from dyes or metallic components.
paragraphs: Fluorescent materials usually emit a single consistent color. They are typically made from dyes or metallic components. In contrast, researchers reporting in ACS Central Science have created carbon dots that can fluoresce in a range of colors under UV light, depending on the concentration and the liquid they're in. The team incorporated the new carbon dots into plastic decorations and used them to create a data encryption system.

LEDs, solar cells and some data protection or anticounterfeiting technologies rely on materials that absorb invisible UV light and then emit visible, colored light. But their glow is usually a single distinct color—think of the bright blue of white clothing or teeth under a blacklight. Siyu Lu, Lin Ai and colleagues wanted to make more versatile fluorescent materials that shift between different colors in response to their surroundings. They were especially interested in these materials for environmental sensing and dynamic information encryption.

The researchers turned to carbon dots—tiny particles that can fluoresce brightly and whose surfaces are adjustable. By tuning those surfaces, they found that the same dot could fluoresce in different colors in varying conditions.

First, the researchers heated two carbon-based compounds in an organic solvent under pressure, forming particles with carbon-rich cores and chemically responsive surfaces. They made two versions, CD1 and CD2, using different ratios of the starting materials.

In tests, CD1 fluoresced red in acidic water and green in alkaline water. Shifting the pH caused the color change to reverse repeatedly without changing the dots' brightness. Similarly, when suspending CD1 and CD2 in different liquids—for example, water, toluene, methanol and ethanol—or varying the dots' concentration, the researchers observed that the dots changed their fluorescence, emitting colors from blue to red.

Next, the researchers mixed carbon dot solutions with polymers to make blue, green, yellow and red materials. They incorporated carbon dot-polymer powders into crafts, including molded Chinese characters and decorative bottles, and folded flexible films into different shapes.

They also used the dots' color changes to create a multidimensional encryption system, encoding information through unique light, liquid and acidity conditions. Together, these findings demonstrate potential uses of the new carbon dots in data security and anticounterfeiting technologies.
"This offers a new approach to designing smart optical materials that can sense their surroundings and convey information," says Lu, a corresponding author of the study.

The researchers are "actively exploring opportunities to commercialize the CDs, particularly for information encryption," says Lu. Next, they will evaluate long-term stability, large-scale manufacturing and production cost.

articles.title: A new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit
articles.dek: A recent study published in Nature Electronics and carried out by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware research group, Quantum Motion, London Center for…
paragraphs: A recent study published in Nature Electronics and carried out by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware research group, Quantum Motion, London Center for Nanotechnology, Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge introduces a new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit fabricated in a commercial complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) process.

Superinductors are electrical inductors that are engineered to have an extremely large inductance, often far beyond what can be achieved with conventional coils. They are particularly important for superconducting qubits and quantum circuits, as a large inductance can dramatically alter the circuit's quantum behavior. This makes superinductors interesting for quantum technology, as they enable the creation of circuits with very large impedance and very small inductive energy scales.

In this work, researchers show that superconducting circuit elements can be fabricated with a commercial CMOS process by utilizing titanium nitride (TiN). TiN is particularly well suited for this purpose because of its high kinetic inductance, which makes it possible to create compact, high-inductance circuit elements while maintaining robust superconducting properties.

The work has reported the development of a nonlinear superinductor within a silicon integrated circuit. The system can be used to create a radiofrequency single-electron transistor—a widely used sensor for semiconductor spin qubits —with a compact footprint and high sensitivity. The next step will be to integrate the resonator with multi-gate transistors to demonstrate high-speed, high-fidelity spin readout well below the microsecond timescale.

However, according to the research team, "the applications of the TiN-based CMOS inductors could expand well beyond quantum sensing and computing for spin qubits, impacting areas such as radio astronomy, low-power cryoelectronics and quantum sensing and simulations."

articles.title: Feejee Mermaid on display in Colorado may shock and intrigue—but no longer considered a 'missing link'
articles.dek: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries.
paragraphs: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshiped Oannes , a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology ; and fairy tales such as " The Little Mermaid " have made this figure a pop culture icon.

During the 1800s, American showman P. T. Barnum brought the Feejee Mermaid to the American public. Presented at the American Museum, run by Barnum in Manhattan from 1841 to 1865 , as " The Greatest Curiosity in the World " and said to have originated in the "Feejee Islands," the creature inspired debates about science and evolution. Some people believed it was a missing link in the evolutionary chain between aquatic and terrestrial life.

I recently viewed a Feejee Mermaid replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science as part of the " Mythic Creatures: Dragons, Unicorns and Mermaids" temporary exhibit . As a folklorist , I'm intrigued by how this mermaid subverted Americans' expectations that mermaids are alluring and how it sparked an interplay between science and myth.

A Feejee Mermaid is a type of traditional art form that originated in Japan and the East Indies more than 400 years ago. It came to Americans in 1842, when Barnum claimed to display a "specimen" at the American Museum in New York City.

In the Japanese version, the lower half was a fish attached to an upper half of a monkey or made of papier-mâché. Barnum's was a mixture of a monkey and a fish, but the replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science has a papier-mâché upper half. Feejee Mermaids were often preserved by being coated in clay .

Mammalian-fish hybrid creatures have a role in Japanese folklore through the ningyo, which is a mermaidlike yokai, a supernatural being thought to have the power to either curse or grant eternal life. Unlike Western mermaids, ningyo were grotesque.

The Feejee Mermaid that became part of Barnum's exhibition was created by a Japanese fisherman in the early 19th century. He claimed to have caught the specimen and said it prophesied a sterility epidemic. The only cure for the townsfolk, the fisherman said, came through owning a picture of the mermaid.
Samuel Barrett Eades, an American sailor, purchased the Feejee Mermaid and willed it to his son, who then sold it to Moses Kimball , a curator at the Boston Museum, in 1842.
In his autobiography, Barnum details the scheme he devised after Kimball showed him the Feejee Mermaid.

Barnum sent letters to newspapers, describing how a "Dr. Griffin," who was really his hoaxing accomplice Levi Lyman, was in possession of the mermaid skeleton. He further spread the word by distributing thousands of pamphlets throughout New York City that detailed when the mermaid would be on display and highlighted the seductive nature of mermaids.
However, when the public arrived at the American Museum, much to their surprise, they found Barnum's grotesque version.

Barnum himself described it as "an ugly dried-up, black-looking diminutive specimen, about three feet (0. 9 meters) long. Its mouth was open, its tail turned over and its arms thrown up, giving it the appearance of having died in great agony."

articles.title: Why one positive E. coli sample put a Pittsburgh-area community under a boil-water advisory
articles.dek: A boil-water advisory was issued on Nov. 2, 2026, by officials in Center Township in Beaver County, 25 miles from Pittsburgh, after a routine sample tested positive for…
paragraphs: A boil-water advisory was issued on Nov. 2, 2026, by officials in Center Township in Beaver County, 25 miles from Pittsburgh, after a routine sample tested positive for coliform bacteria, including E. coli , according to the township’s water authority .

The advisory stayed in place while the authority kept testing, and Central Valley School District students stayed out of school buildings and attended class remotely on Nov. 3-4 as a precaution. The authority lifted the advisory on Nov. 4.
A single positive sample of E. coli can upend daily routines for an entire community, from what people drink to how they wash dishes, and leave residents wondering how worried they should be.
Two environmental engineers, Sarah Fakhreddine and Marlee Shaffer , explain why E. coli in tap water is a red flag, how boiling kills harmful germs, and how utilities decide the water is safe again.

When E. coli is detected in a drinking-water system, it means the water may contain harmful bacteria, viruses or parasites. Most strains of E. coli don’t make people sick, but E. coli is a common bacterium that lives in the digestive systems of people and animals. That’s why scientists use it as an indicator: Its presence flags that water has been contaminated by human or animal waste, which can carry germs that do cause illness.

A drinking-water system treats water so it is safe for people to drink and delivers that clean water to customers’ taps. Water can become contaminated during treatment or delivery, as it moves through the system’s pipes.

If there’s a problem with the treatment process, harmful pathogens may not be fully removed from the water. Or treatment may be working well, but a pipe breaks somewhere in the system and pressure drops. That can allow contaminated water to enter the pipes that deliver water to homes and businesses.

The U. S. Environmental Protection Agency sets a goal of zero E. coli in drinking water. A single water sample is a snapshot of water quality at the time and place it was collected. Because drinking water systems are interconnected, with water flowing through them, a problem in one location might mean water elsewhere could also be contaminated.

How much of the system is affected depends on where and why the problem occurred. It can take time for a utility to find the problem, fix it and test more water samples. A boil-water advisory helps keep the public safe while the utility investigates and addresses the problem.

Boiling water kills harmful bacteria and protozoa and inactivates viruses that might be in the water. High temperatures damage key structural parts of these microorganisms, leaving them unable to multiply and cause infections.

Research shows that at the temperatures water reaches when it boils, most harmful microbes are killed in under a minute. It can also help to keep some bottled water on hand in case you are unable to boil water.

Water utilities must show the water is safe and get approval before lifting a boil-water advisory. They have to investigate what caused the E. coli contamination, fix the problem and then keep testing to make sure no more samples come back positive. They share this information with their state or federal regulatory agency, which decides whether the utility has met the requirements to lift the advisory.
In Pennsylvania, the state Department of Environmental Protection requires a utility to show two consecutive days of negative samples after addressing the problem.

In a school cafeteria, for example, an advisory affects not just drinking water but also the water used to wash fruits and vegetables, cook food and wash dishes. Meeting those requirements can be challenging, depending on the school’s size, its resources and whether it can get other sources of water, such as bottled water that has been transported in by truck.

Some schools may be able to stay open and comply with the advisory, while others may decide to close or switch to virtual learning to ensure safety. Children can be more vulnerable than healthy adults to waterborne illnesses , so compliance by schools is especially important.

articles.title: NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon
articles.dek: In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.
paragraphs: In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.

Agency leadership provided updates on the previously announced acceleration plans for the Artemis program, advancing toward the agency’s Artemis III test flight in 2027 and Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028. Building on the priorities announced at Ignition earlier this year, NASA leadership shared the agency’s significant progress across its missions, working with industry partners to test critical capabilities, reduce risk, and build toward a sustained American presence on the Moon.

“This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible,” said Isaacman. “NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we’re not waiting for others to bring their plans to us — the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.”

The agency shared details of the Artemis III mission, which will test rendezvous, docking, and operations between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar lander test vehicles from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit. Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, launched on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission.

The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence: Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship.

The Oct. 23 updates follow other recent updates about the Artemis missions. Hardware for Artemis III is on track, with processing timelines sharply reduced by about half. NASA also redesigned, built, and tested a critical fuel-line component in-house in five months, at roughly a tenth of the cost of an earlier outside-vendor estimate.

“NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it,” said Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager. “It’s an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.”

For the agency’s Artemis IV mission in 2028, astronauts will launch aboard Orion on the SLS rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop lunar landers to carry those astronauts to the Moon’s surface. Both companies have redesigned their approaches to simplify the missions and make them more efficient and flexible as compared to previous mission designs.

SpaceX’s Starship will refuel in Earth orbit, rendezvous with Orion, and then carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Blue Origin’s approach involves transfer stages in Earth orbit to push its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander toward the Moon, where it will meet Orion in a closer lunar orbit before descending to the surface.
Both SpaceX and Blue Origin are targeting to be able to support a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

For Artemis IV, NASA is pursuing two upper-stage options for the SLS rocket: its current stage, the interim cryogenic propulsion stage; and a stretched version of ULA’s Centaur V which can carry more propellant. Pursuing both options ensures NASA is maintaining flexibility and preventing single-point dependency.

NASA also announced plans with spacesuit provider Axiom Space to develop a second, lighter suit design called the “Sortie suit” to enable the first moonwalks. The Sortie suit will not replace Axiom’s primary suit, which will be used for longer, more demanding missions in the future. The Sortie suit is roughly half the weight of the larger suit and lets NASA move faster on the earliest surface missions.

articles.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe Discovers Something Unexpected Hidden in the Chaos of Space
articles.dek: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has uncovered hidden order in space turbulence, a finding that could help scientists understand magnetic storms on Earth.
paragraphs: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has uncovered hidden order in space turbulence, a finding that could help scientists understand magnetic storms on Earth.

Smoke rising from an incense stick can begin as a thin, steady stream before curling and spreading unpredictably. The smoke makes turbulence in the air visible. Turbulence also occurs in space, where the moving material is plasma, an ionized gas containing electrically charged particles. Electric and magnetic fields strongly influence how those particles move, making this turbulence different from the movements of ordinary air.

Space plasma is also so dilute that its particles rarely collide, making it effectively collisionless. Physicists are still working to understand how turbulence develops under these conditions and how its energy is distributed. Measurements from NASA’s Parker Solar Probe have now revealed an organized pattern within that irregular activity.

At large scales, plasma behaves like a fluid, and turbulence develops through swirling motions called vortices and through electromagnetic waves. The fluctuations become random. At smaller scales, the dynamics of individual particles become important. These are different ways the same material behaves depending on the size of the disturbances being examined.

Picture the magnetic field’s direction as an arrow that can turn as the field fluctuates. Viewed looking radially away from the Sun, the fields preferentially rotate counterclockwise at larger scales. At smaller scales, they rotate clockwise.

The reversal occurs at the wavelength, or spatial scale, where fluid-like behavior gives way to particle-like dynamics. Farther from the Sun, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths, corresponding to larger spatial scales.

“We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions,” says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa of Technische Universität Braunschweig (TU Braunschweig), the article’s first author.

The study brought together researchers from the Institute of Theoretical Physics at TU Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, in cooperation with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other research institutes. The collaboration spanned ten countries, and the results are published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters .
Dr. Yokoi of the University of Tokyo says, “The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics.”

Plasma turbulence plays an important role in the solar wind, solar eruptions, and interplanetary space, as well as in Earth’s magnetosphere, the region dominated by our planet’s magnetic field. It also matters in accretion disks, where material orbits and moves inward toward a central object. In interplanetary space, turbulence can influence the shock waves and magnetic clouds produced by solar eruptions, making it an important factor in predicting geomagnetic storms.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite
articles.dek: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth.
paragraphs: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions .

Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September . The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.
As a Ph. D. candidate in aerospace engineering , I know that rescuing satellites is hard . I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.

Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem.

The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface, where it could keep observing for years.

In late July, LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels , which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel. That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin.
Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant.

Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by firing its thrusters against the spin . NASA reported in August that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second.

NASA and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost later in August . The team still flew LINK within 7. 5 to 9 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters. It never got close enough to grab the telescope.

A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant. Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission’s jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit. They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises.
Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch. Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home.

That scenario is close to what happened to LINK. Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft no longer had enough propellant to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely.

A fuel budget that covers only the planned steps leaves nothing for recovering from a fault. But every extra pound of propellant also makes a spacecraft heavier, and heavier spacecraft cost more to launch and take more fuel to move.

Starting in 2024, solar activity swelled Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the extra drag pulled Swift down faster than expected. Once NASA saw how quickly Swift was falling, the agency had to move fast to try to save the observatory. Space missions typically take years to develop and launch, but in this case, a slow, conventional development program risked arriving too late.
NASA awarded Katalyst a US$30 million contract in September 2025. The company had less than a year to design, build, test and launch LINK . LINK launched on July 3, 2026.

Speed comes with trade-offs. In engineering, a compressed schedule can leave less time for repeated testing, building spare hardware and planning recovery options. Public reports do not say whether that trade-off played any part in LINK’s faults.

NASA has said that even though LINK didn’t succeed, the effort gave the agency experience in quickly building, launching and operating a servicing spacecraft. Engineers also showed they could upload new control software to steady a damaged servicing spacecraft with the hardware it had left. And LINK tested its arms and fired all three thrusters at once in orbit.

While Swift was the most pressing case for a boost mission, it’s not the only one. NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope could one day use a similar boost, and news reports suggested it would have been next in line had this mission worked.

Future missions are pursuing two complementary approaches for rescuing satellites. Astroscale’s ELSA-M is built to capture satellites that carry a docking plate installed before launch, which would make it easier for a rescuer to snag and boost them if the satellite eventually got into trouble. The European Space Agency’s ClearSpace-1 is planned for 2029 and aims to capture the Proba-1 satellite, which doesn’t have a docking plate or anything to help ClearSpace-1 capture it, and remove it from orbit.

LINK’s mission showed that a rescue takes more than a robotic arm and enough thrust to reach a target. It also takes a servicer spacecraft that can stay stable, recover from its own faults and keep enough propellant reserved to finish the job. In Swift’s case, the rescuer fell short before the rescue could begin.

articles.title: Pennsylvania Democrats now have power to push forward on election reform, marijuana legalization and minimum wage increases
articles.dek: The 2026 midterm elections changed the balance of power in Washington, D. C. It also proved to be a pivotal election in Pennsylvania.
paragraphs: The 2026 midterm elections changed the balance of power in Washington, D. C. It also proved to be a pivotal election in Pennsylvania.

Gov. Josh Shapiro handily defeated Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Not only that, it looks like Democrats will expand their majority in the state House and have flipped the state Senate , earning a 26-24 majority.
That gives Shapiro the coveted party trifecta – single party control of both the governor’s office and the General Assembly.
Given the pent-up demand among Democrats who have not fully controlled Harrisburg for over 30 years , the excitement is palpable among Pennsylvania Democrats.

I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics . Now that the political fault lines are clear for the next two years in Pennsylvania’s state government, it is worth considering what Democrats may do with their newfound power.
For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate.
Election reform has been a perennial priority in Pennsylvania since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election.

Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting where voters could vote all at once for a single party, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.

Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties in Pennsylvania to use ballot drop boxes , maintain no-excuse mail-in voting , set clear rules for ballot curing where voters are able to correct issues with their submitted mail ballots instead of having them invalidated, institute precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allow independents to vote in open primary elections .
Democrats may now be able to pass all of these without having to compromise with Republican demands for stricter voter ID requirements.

Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House passed a legalization bill in 2025 . Democrats had said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they took the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization remain to be worked out, even with Democratic control.
Democrats have sponsored divergent bills on whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores , similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania.

Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the war on drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things such as expungements of past convictions, setting aside licenses for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues.

Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details. But a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania makes it even more likely that the commonwealth will be among the next states where adult-use recreational marijuana is legal.

The House has passed several measures to regulate artificial intelligence and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs , water use , local government authority and implementing and the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan.

These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda. Additionally, criticism over the AI-generated ads fielded by the Garrity campaign , which are regulated in other states , may add this issue to the state’s AI policy agenda.

Given that this election was likely heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability , Democrats will need to show progress on bringing down prices where they can. The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.

Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7. 25 minimum hourly wage over time. The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it also had been passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage. The legislation will have to be introduced and passed again by the new General Assembly.

Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges decision by the U. S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent.

Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up and may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult , constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights.

Pennsylvania also does not include LGBTQ individuals in its nondiscrimination protections. The Democrats in the House passed a bill that would add sexual orientation and gender identity to the state’s Human Relations Act in 2026, but it also died in the Senate. Democrats are likely to pick this up again in 2027.
Ultimately, Democrats will not be able to do everything. They will need to decide what to prioritize and what to leave behind.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Is About to Become the First Spacecraft One Light-Day From Earth
articles.dek: Voyager 1 is nearing a distance from Earth that light takes a full day to cross, while NASA engineers stretch its dwindling power to keep it exploring.
paragraphs: Voyager 1 is nearing a distance from Earth that light takes a full day to cross, while NASA engineers stretch its dwindling power to keep it exploring.

NASA’s Voyager 1, humanity’s most distant spacecraft, was about 16 billion miles (25. 75 billion kilometers) from Earth when its radio signal disappeared in October. NASA’s Deep Space Network , which uses large antennas at three facilities around the globe to communicate with spacecraft at the Moon and beyond, could not detect the probe during two scheduled contacts on October 18 and 19, 24 hours apart.
The signal returned on October 20, ending the 48-hour interruption before engineers had sent commands to troubleshoot the problem. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 since then.

Engineers are still investigating what caused the communication loss. They have determined that one group of thrusters went offline and its backups switched on. Thrusters are small rocket engines used to control a spacecraft’s movement or orientation. Voyager 1 is programmed to make the switch automatically if its computers detect something wrong with the active thrusters. This response, called fault protection, puts the spacecraft into a safe, stable configuration and pauses normal operations, giving engineers time to diagnose the problem and act.

“This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.”

Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are the only spacecraft ever to study interstellar space directly. Both now travel beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun. Keeping their instruments running preserves access to measurements that no other spacecraft can provide.

Both probes draw electricity from radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which convert heat from decaying plutonium into electrical power. As that fuel supply diminishes, each spacecraft loses about 4 watts of power a year. Nearly half a century after the mission’s 1977 launch, little spare power remains, and engineers have been shutting down nonessential devices and systems to conserve energy.

The mission began with 10 dedicated science instruments . Some were shut down after the spacecraft completed their planetary encounters, while others stayed on to study the heliosphere’s outer region. In recent years, dwindling power has forced the team to turn off two science instruments.

Saving electricity also requires keeping the spacecraft warm enough to work. In early September, engineers completed a months-long effort to turn off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replace their functions with three lower-power alternatives. The operation, nicknamed the “Big Bang,” came about six weeks after the team performed the same swap on Voyager 2 .

All six devices involved help keep the spacecraft warm in the cold of space. To reduce electricity use while maintaining the proper distribution of heat, engineers had to make all three swaps simultaneously. The successful operation will allow Voyager 1’s remaining science instruments to work longer than previously anticipated. Without it, the team would have needed to shut down another instrument as early as summer 2027.

Voyager 1 is traveling at 38,000 mph (61,155 kph) toward another milestone. On November 18, it will be 16. 09 billion miles (25. 89 billion kilometers) from Earth. That distance equals one light-day, the distance light travels in a day. A radio message from Earth will take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and its reply will need another 24 hours to travel back.
Crossing that threshold will cause no change in the spacecraft’s surroundings or anything aboard it. The milestone marks the reach and endurance of humanity’s most distant explorer.
“If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.

articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.dek: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “ It’s the…
paragraphs: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “ It’s the economy, stupid .” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy , making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D. C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think , because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers , with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz , which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food , follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally .

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection . For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record .
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U. S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month , and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4. 31 to $10. 31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U. S. gasoline prices from increasing 32% .
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12. 3% , and gas prices were still high .
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “ Whip Inflation Now ,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3. 49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U. S. stayed high and even climbed slightly . Inflation hit 9% in 1978 .

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats . Inflation continued to climb , and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976 . Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “ Reaganomics ” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum . By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U. S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut , lowering the average price of crude oil and U. S. gasoline price from previous highs .
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22% . In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate .

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U. S. economy. U. S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40% . Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U. S. rose by 66%, from $2. 11 to $3. 52 per gallon .
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0. 17 to $0. 42 per gallon .

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U. S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U. S. to the Paris climate accord , under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9. 1% , a 40-year high. And U. S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4. 929 per gallon ; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5. 60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4. 5% , U. S. oil production rose 3. 3% , from 13. 3 million to 13. 7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4. 5%, from $3. 12 to $2. 98 per gallon .

articles.title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
articles.dek: NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring…
paragraphs: NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems.
Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace.

The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029.
The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are:

Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services.

articles.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
articles.dek: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.
paragraphs: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.

An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution ( SPLICE ) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California.

During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data.

Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed the SPLICE payload and partnered with specialists at NASA Armstrong to integrate, test, and fly it aboard the Alta-X drone in June and July. Those tests verified communications, data handling, telemetry, and command- control performance between the SPLICE payload and the drone to prepare for a full-scale test at Voyager Technologies in Mojave, California, later this month.

“This flight test is the culmination of almost a decade of work, for the SPLICE project,” said Davis Adams, NASA project manager. “This flight raised the technology readiness level, priming it for integration into future robotic and crewed lunar flights. Validation of the guidance and navigation systems are applicable to terrestrial, lunar, and Martian descent and landing missions.”

NASA has worked with a number of commercial lunar lander providers to implement iterations of SPLICE into their platforms. A number of the landers slated for upcoming Moon Base missions leverage data collected by NASA through the development of systems like SPLICE to execute soft touchdowns on the lunar surface.

“We are coordinating with industry regarding the usage of the guidance system once the system is available in the NASA software catalog, currently planned for this fall,” Adams said. “Some of the companies also are evaluating the system’s navigation capabilities for precision landing applications, as well as potential extensions for autonomous surface mobility.”

NASA’s Flight Opportunities project, based at NASA Armstrong, enabled flight testing of the SPLICE project early in its development that laid a foundation for it to continue advancing its technology readiness level to what it is today. Flight testing included both a descent altitude and a landing trajectory in 2019 similar to what is expected on a lunar mission and the demonstration of two NASA-developed precision landing sensor systems in 2020.

articles.title: A Woman Who Lived 30,000 Years Ago Is Changing What We Know About Ice Age Europe
articles.dek: DNA preserved in ancient cave sediments reveals how some Ice Age Europeans endured extreme cold, while genetic evidence from France uncovers unexpected connections across the…
paragraphs: DNA preserved in ancient cave sediments reveals how some Ice Age Europeans endured extreme cold, while genetic evidence from France uncovers unexpected connections across the continent.

A woman who lived in southwestern France around 30,000 years ago carried a genetic history that stretched far beyond her corner of Ice Age Europe. Most of her ancestry was western European, but part of it was related to populations in central and eastern Europe. Her DNA challenges the idea that ancient populations on opposite sides of the continent remained largely separated from one another.

For archaeologists, evidence of these distant connections is not entirely new. The Gravettian culture, which spread across Europe roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago, left behind evidence suggesting extensive contact between groups. Ancient DNA, however, seemed to tell a different story, pointing to relatively stable eastern and western ancestry groups. The two lines of evidence had been difficult to reconcile.

Now, an international research team led by the University of Vienna has found genetic evidence that helps bring those pictures together. In a study published in Science Advances , researchers combined new and previously published genomes with human DNA recovered from cave sediments, uncovering evidence of both long-distance genetic exchange and populations that endured in the same regions for thousands of years.

The clearest evidence of those distant connections came from a woman whose remains were discovered at Isturitz Cave in southwestern France. Her remains yielded the oldest genome-wide dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe. Genetic modeling places the exchange between eastern and western populations around 32,500 to 31,500 years ago, before she lived.

“Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed,” says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. “Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected.”

She was not the only person to carry evidence of these connections. A previously studied individual from Ormesson, France, showed a similar genetic signal. When considered alongside archaeological findings, the results also strengthen the possibility that Isturitz served as a meeting place for different groups, although the DNA cannot reveal exactly how those encounters occurred.

Yet contact across Europe did not necessarily mean that established populations disappeared or were replaced. In northern Spain, researchers uncovered another part of the story: western European ancestry persisted for thousands of years, including through some of the harshest conditions of the last Ice Age.

Genomic evidence from Chufín Cave points to this long-term continuity. At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, the researchers went a step further, recovering human genetic information without relying on bones or teeth. A sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years contained enough human nuclear DNA to identify the genetic ancestry of people who had occupied the cave, despite the absence of human skeletal remains in that layer.

The DNA revealed that western European ancestry had persisted through the Last Glacial Maximum, when Ice Age conditions were particularly severe. Together with the evidence from Chufín, this supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula served as a refuge where human populations endured during a period of extreme cold.

“Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”

In southern Italy, the team examined a different aspect of ancient population life through the remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus who was most likely the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1. Genetic analysis suggests that his father probably belonged to the same population as his mother, yet the parents were not closely related. The researchers interpret this as a possible sign of mating practices that helped prevent high levels of inbreeding, even among people who shared a common genetic background.

articles.title: NASA Space Grant Students Fuel Agency’s Inspiration Tour
articles.dek: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies,…
paragraphs: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action.

In Iowa, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman toured the Make to Innovate program lab at Iowa State University. Students from the Iowa Space Grant Consortium’s Mission Moon program, along with consortium-funded student organizations including Cardinal Space Mining, CySat, and CyLaunch, shared research findings and demonstrated the institution’s strong connection to NASA via agency-funded projects. During a well-attended town hall event NASA experts briefed students on the agency’s Moon Base efforts and how their work can contribute to future exploration.

“We’re grateful for the opportunity to welcome NASA leadership to Iowa State,” said Sara Nelson Iowa Space Grant director. “The excitement among students was incredible, and the visit highlighted how the research and innovation happening in Iowa can help advance Artemis and NASA’s future exploration efforts.”

At the University of Arizona, the NASA administrator saw firsthand the space research and engineering capabilities that are enabled by the Arizona Space Grant Consortium. From satellite communications testing to complex optics for peering into deep space to student-built high-altitude balloon payloads and even small satellites, students at the University of Arizona have a long history of contributing to NASA missions and making aerospace career connections. This tour stop also included a Q&A session where the NASA administrator answered questions from local high school and college students.

“It was incredible to present the high-altitude ballooning research we do in SEDS (Students for the Exploration and Development of Space) to Jared Isaacman and those at NASA,” said Ella Miller, a junior studying mechanical engineering at the University of Arizona. “Arizona Space Grant has allowed me to get hands-on experience through an entire mission design process every semester, helping me pursue a career in space research and secure internships in this field.”

At the University of Alaska in Fairbanks, the Administrator toured two Geophysical Institute facilities: Poker Flat Research Range, the university’s scientific rocket launching facility, and the Alaska Satellite Facility. During an Alaska Space Grant science fair, students shared research in hibernation biology and showcased CubeSat technology advancements. Students were also able to learn about the agency’s Moon Base program and ask questions about opportunities available to the next generation of innovators and explorers.

In North Dakota, the Inspiration Tour focused on future exploration capabilities. Space Grant-funded research at the University of North Dakota is helping to shape the future of exploration across STEM fields. Student fellows and NASA interns shared their projects on supercell mergers using satellite imagery, geomagnetic conditions of aurora borealis, and in-situ resource utilization, to name a few. North Dakota Space Grant STEM ambassador students also shared robotics and drone activities as part of “Mission Moon”, which centers Artemis initiatives in statewide collaborations with educators and other North Dakota colleges and universities.

“Getting to speak with the NASA Administrator was an amazing opportunity!” said research fellow and STEM ambassador Malissa Reinhardt. “He genuinely cared about what we students had to say and the research we’re working on, which makes all the hard work we put into our research and North Dakota Space Grant Consortium so rewarding.”

NASA’s Inspiration Tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public showcase of air and space innovation on Nov. 7 and 8, highlighting the agency’s commitment to preparing the next generation of innovators and explorers for humanity’s next giant leap. As NASA enters a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, the national network of Space Grant consortia is expanding opportunities for students to lead the way in an aerospace workforce that is evolving and growing. At learning institutions from coast to coast, today’s Space Grant students are launching America’s future in space.

articles.title: 33 Out of 34 Lupus Patients Shared an Immune Cell Abnormality
articles.dek: New research challenges a longstanding explanation for why the immune system attacks healthy tissues in lupus.
paragraphs: New research challenges a longstanding explanation for why the immune system attacks healthy tissues in lupus.

Scientists investigating lupus have discovered that errors in immune cells may cause the body to attack some of its own defenses. In a study of 34 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), 33 had neutrophils containing widespread abnormalities in RNA processing. These changes were absent from blood samples taken from healthy volunteers.

Neutrophils normally help defend the body against infections, but the altered cells produced unusual molecules that other immune cells appeared to recognize as threats. Researchers at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and the University of Washington (UW) found evidence that both T cells and antibody-producing B cells could participate in this response, potentially contributing to the inflammation and tissue damage associated with lupus.

The abnormalities involve RNA “splicing,” a process that allows cells to remove unnecessary sections of genetic instructions before using them to produce proteins. In the lupus patients, errors caused sections of RNA to be joined incorrectly. When cells attempted to “read” these altered instructions, they generated unusual peptides, short chains of amino acids that can be recognized by the immune system.

T cells routinely inspect peptides displayed on cell surfaces to identify infections and other threats. When they encounter unfamiliar or “foreign” peptides, especially in the presence of inflammation, they may respond as though they have detected a pathogen. These molecular targets are known as “antigens.” Peptides produced through abnormal RNA processing can become “neoantigens,” potentially making the body’s own cells targets of an immune response.

“When a cell type whose function is pro-inflammatory, such as neutrophils, also expresses potentially immunogenic mutations, the conditions for immune attack are met: T cells sense a foreign antigen plus inflammation or ‘danger’ signals,” explains LJI Professor Stephen Schoenberger, Ph. D.

The findings, published in Nature , emerged from a collaboration between Schoenberger and UW School of Medicine Professor Tomas Mustelin, M. D. , Ph. D. Mustelin’s laboratory had identified unusually frequent RNA splicing errors in neutrophils from lupus patients. Schoenberger, whose research focuses on immune recognition of mutation-derived antigens, investigated whether those errors could produce molecules capable of provoking an immune response.

Schoenberger has previously studied neoantigens in cancer, where mutations can create abnormal molecules that help immune cells recognize and attack tumors. Applying similar methods to lupus, the researchers found that altered neutrophils expressed numerous neoantigens that could alert the immune system. They also identified evidence that B cells, which produce antibodies, were prepared to respond to the affected cells.
“This may get to the very crux of the disease pathogenesis,” says Schoenberger, referring to the biological processes responsible for lupus.

Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease in which immune activity can damage joints, skin, kidneys, and other organs. Scientists have long investigated why T cells and B cells begin attacking the body’s own tissues. One explanation involves a breakdown of immune “tolerance,” the mechanisms that normally prevent immune cells from responding to healthy tissues.

The new findings support an alternative possibility known as the “neoantigen hypothesis” of autoimmunity. Rather than mistakenly recognizing normal cellular components as dangerous, immune cells may encounter genuinely unfamiliar molecules generated within the body. Their responses could therefore follow the same biological rules used to recognize foreign threats.

“Rather than a failure of immune tolerance, autoimmunity can be caused by the immune system doing exactly what it’s supposed to do, which is to mount an attack on non-self, on things that are foreign,” says Schoenberger.

Although the researchers identified a potential mechanism for immune “self-attack,” they have not established whether abnormal RNA splicing helps initiate lupus or develops in response to existing inflammation. Neutrophils are already known to contribute to the complex immune processes that sustain the disease.

“Neutrophils clearly participate in a self-amplifying inflammatory circuit in SLE, involving autoantibodies, immune complexes, nucleic acids, type I interferons, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs),” says Schoenberger. “So now the big question is whether neoantigens are a cause or consequence of this process? Neutrophils might be responding to inflammation that’s already causing tissue damage.”

articles.title: Common Nutritional Supplement Shows Surprising Promise Against Psoriasis
articles.dek: A widely available nutritional supplement may help reduce the immune system activity responsible for psoriasis, according to new research from China.
paragraphs: A widely available nutritional supplement may help reduce the immune system activity responsible for psoriasis, according to new research from China. Scientists found that pantethine, a derivative of vitamin B5 commonly used to lower cholesterol, can interfere with metabolic processes that drive inflammation. The findings were supported by experiments in mice and a small clinical trial involving people with psoriasis.

In the 12-week trial, 24 patients received standard treatment with topical calcipotriene/betamethasone ointment. Half also took pantethine tablets. Participants receiving the supplement showed improvements in their symptoms, particularly those who started with elevated blood cholesterol levels. Although encouraging, the results are preliminary and do not establish pantethine as an effective standalone treatment.

The research focused on dendritic cells, immune cells that help organize the body’s defenses. These cells detect and present foreign substances to specialized T cells and release chemical signals that recruit other immune cells. When dendritic cells become excessively active, they can sustain the inflammation associated with psoriasis and other autoimmune diseases.

The scientists discovered unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from patients with psoriasis and several other autoimmune conditions. Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient involved in cellular energy production. The researchers found that increased Vanin activity depleted pantethine, promoting cholesterol production within dendritic cells and triggering excessive immune activation.

“Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression,” says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. “But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.”

To investigate this connection, the researchers reduced Vanin levels in dendritic cells. Without these enzymes, the cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. A drug that inhibited Vanins also prevented the development of psoriasis in mice.

Further experiments showed that replenishing pantethine reduced cholesterol accumulation inside dendritic cells and suppressed their activation. Pantethine treatment also alleviated psoriasis symptoms in mice, providing additional evidence that the metabolic pathway contributes to inflammatory disease.

“We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins,” Zhang says.

Pantethine has long been available as a nutritional supplement because it can inhibit cholesterol synthesis. The new findings suggest that its effects on cholesterol metabolism may also influence immune responses. However, the small human trial cannot establish whether the improvements resulted from the same cellular mechanism demonstrated in laboratory experiments.

“Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation,” Zhang says. “Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell–mediated autoimmune diseases.”
