articles.title: How a French philosopher’s warnings about speed and power describe today’s AI race
articles.dek: With the race to build artificial intelligence systems smarter than any human has come a boom in “accidents.”
paragraphs: With the race to build artificial intelligence systems smarter than any human has come a boom in “accidents.” In a safety test run by the company Anthropic , its own AI agent blackmailed an engineer to avoid being shut down. Criminals have used AI agents for data-extortion campaigns and to hack government agencies , banks and technology companies. In other tests, models have escaped from test environments into real organizational systems .

Several researchers who resigned from leading AI companies in 2026 have accused their employers of not taking the dangers seriously enough . In September, Bill Gates told “Meet the Press” that AI is “ powerful enough to drive events that can cause a billion deaths .”

Paul Virilio, a French philosopher, spent his career analyzing the relationships between technology, speed and power . He died in 2018 , well before generative AI and the fears about it reached their present pitch. But I doubt much would have surprised him.

As a researcher who studies AI-generated media and how people make sense of it, I find that three of Virilio’s ideas explain today’s AI moment better than anything written since. He argued that every new technology brings a new kind of accident into the world ; that speed takes away our time to think ; and that globally connected systems can fail everywhere at once.

Virilio was born in Paris in 1932. When World War II began, his family moved to Nantes, a port city near the Atlantic. During the Nazi occupation of France, Germany began building the Atlantic Wall , a series of defensive fortifications stretching along the coast from Spain to Norway.

But in September 1943, when he was 11, Virilio saw what the wall could not keep out. American bombers aiming for Nantes’ port hit the city center instead , killing about 1,400 people and destroying more than 700 buildings in two raids.
“War was my university,” he told an interviewer . “Everything has proceeded from there.”

As a young man, Virilio spent years photographing the abandoned bunkers of the Atlantic Wall. The lesson he drew from them was about speed: The Germans had built a massive military fortification, yet the Allies had gone over and around it; the wall barely slowed them.
Walls were a technology of space, and the bombers were a technology of speed – inspiring his philosophical approach to understanding the world.
As an adult, Virilio studied many more examples of technological failures, such as the Chernobyl power plant meltdown of 1986, the worst nuclear accident in history.

In his 2005 book “ The Original Accident ,” Virilio summed up his main idea in a simple sentence: “To invent the sailing ship or steamer is to invent the shipwreck.” The train invents derailment; the airplane, the crash; the nuclear plant, the meltdown. Every invention, not just dangerous ones, carries a specific kind of failure that did not exist before it.

In Virilio’s telling, the “accident” is not the result of bad luck added afterward. It is born at the moment of invention, even if the inventor cannot see it, because the invention will be used in ways they never imagined.

Virilio did not think such accidents could be avoided. But by carefully watching, he believed, people could contain failure and prevent catastrophe. He argued that societies tend to treat each disaster as a one-off, grieve it on television, and forget it, so that the next technology’s accident arrives as a surprise.

In 2002, he staged a Paris exhibition as a trial run for his plan to build a “Museum of Accidents.” Collecting information about shipwrecks, plane crashes, industrial disasters and financial crashes side by side, he argued, would show the pattern: that every invention has its failure and that failure can be anticipated .
AI has invented not one accident but several . Tech companies’ own incident reports form a sort of “museum” – but not an objective one.
Virilio’s second key idea came from the Cold War. In 1977, he published “ Speed and Politics ,” written in a world where nuclear missiles could cross the planet in minutes.

He named the idea “dromology,” derived from the Greek word for a racecourse: “dromos .” Every age runs at the pace of its fastest machine, Virilio wrote, and whatever cannot keep up – including law, deliberation and conscience – drops out of the picture. There is “no democracy, only dromocracy”: the rule of the fastest.

AI can squeeze months of work into hours. In September 2026, Open AI announced that 10,000 of its AI agents had produced a proof of a math problem that had stood for a century – a problem two human mathematicians had spent a year trying to solve .

Virilio’s deepest fear about speed was not that people would fall behind machines, but that they would be absent from decision-making. Even when people attempt to stay in the loop, AI agents execute so quickly that human workers often fail to spot problems or malicious requests .
Virilio’s third idea is the “integral accident”: a failure that, because the same technology runs everywhere, happens everywhere at once .

During the 1990s, Virilio watched how satellite television, the internet and electronic markets let an event anywhere, such as a financial crash, be felt everywhere. He later predicted that in a networked world, integral accidents, not war, would be “ the continuation of politics by other means .”
AI has intensified how tightly connected the world is. It’s being used to help balance power grids , manage ships and harbors , and write hospital patient records .

Consider Anthropic’s Claude Mythos model, which finds security flaws in banking software faster than banks can fix them. Many financial institutions use the same software, so a criminal with such a model could break into multiple banks at the same time.

Virilio wrote that a society that lives only in the present makes accidents more likely . A society too busy to keep records of its past, or to think ahead, cannot learn from its failures and so repeats them.

articles.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
articles.dek: People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount.
paragraphs: People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount.

This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people . The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team.
Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts.

Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies.

To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal , a U. S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank.

We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad.

Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke , a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000.

articles.title: Trapped in Amber for 99 Million Years, a Lizard’s Tail Reveals an Ancient Survival Secret
articles.dek: A clean break in 99-million-year-old amber offers rare direct evidence that ancient lizards shed their tails using a defensive mechanism still common today.
paragraphs: A clean break in 99-million-year-old amber offers rare direct evidence that ancient lizards shed their tails using a defensive mechanism still common today.

A lizard can escape a predator by leaving its tail behind, sometimes with the detached piece still wriggling as the animal makes its getaway. It’s a remarkable defense, but scientists have struggled to determine how far back it goes. Ancient reptile fossils can show where a tail was capable of breaking, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean the animal could shed it to escape danger.

An unusually revealing clue has now emerged from a tiny piece of amber discovered in northern Myanmar. Measuring just 18 millimeters (about 0. 7 inches) long, the amber holds a lizard’s tail that detached approximately 99 million years ago. What makes it so valuable is the remarkably preserved point where the tail separated from the body. Researchers say it provides the best-preserved direct fossil evidence of autotomy, the defensive mechanism that allows lizards to shed their tails.

For years, no one recognized what was trapped inside the amber. Dolev Fabrikant, a PhD candidate at Tel Aviv University’s New Environmental School, was examining what appeared to be a tiny twig or fragment of an insect when he noticed something unusual about its surface. “I realized that what seemed to be a twig was covered in tiny scales,” he recalls. “It was a lizard’s tail.”
Fabrikant shared his discovery with his supervisor, Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology and Steinhardt Museum of Natural History, whose reaction was immediate.

“I nearly jumped out of my chair,” says Dr. Davranoglou. “I instantly realized that this tiny fossil could open an extraordinary window into the past, helping us understand the history of one of the most widespread survival strategies among reptiles. Until now, we could only speculate on whether ancient lizards could shed their tails. We now have direct evidence that one could.”

Getting a closer look at the fossil was another challenge. The amber was cloudy, and the structures inside were too small for an ordinary microscope to reveal the details researchers needed. Rather than cutting open the specimen, the team turned to micro-CT scanning at Israel’s Volcani Institute.

“Micro-CT takes X-ray images from many angles and combines them into a three-dimensional reconstruction. It allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open,” explains Dr. Ahmed Nasser, Head of the institute’s Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.

At the severed end of the tail, the scans revealed a distinctive ring of tissue closely resembling the structure found in tails shed by living lizards. The separation itself was relatively clean and symmetrical, without the damage patterns that would be expected if the tail had broken off in an accident.

That distinction matters because other reptile fossils have offered less conclusive evidence. Some preserve natural fracture planes in the tail vertebrae, while others contain regenerated tails, indicating that the animals had lost part of their tails previously. Although these features suggest that ancient reptiles possessed the ability to shed their tails, the presence of fracture planes alone cannot establish that they actually used this defense. In the Myanmar specimen, the preserved tissue and clean separation provide much stronger evidence that the tail was released through autotomy.

The researchers still cannot determine exactly what kind of lizard left the tail behind. Without the rest of its skeleton, including the skull, there are too few anatomical clues to identify its closest relatives.

“Although we can securely identify this specimen as a lizard, we lack the skull and other skeletal features that would allow a more secure identification. Possible affinities include the groups containing today’s wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards,” says Apostolos Christopoulos, a PhD candidate at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.

How the tail ended up in amber is another mystery. The lizard might have become stuck in sticky resin and shed its tail to free itself. It is also possible that a predator attacked the animal, prompting it to release its tail, which later landed in resin.

articles.title: Before the Dawn in America’s Heartland
articles.dek: The predawn hours brought clear skies over much of the eastern United States on October 18, 2026. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station seized the opportunity…
paragraphs: The predawn hours brought clear skies over much of the eastern United States on October 18, 2026. An astronaut aboard the International Space Station seized the opportunity to capture this wide-angle photo at 4:54 a. m. Central Daylight Time (09:54 Universal Time), with illuminated cities large and small arrayed across the darkened landscape.

The U. S. Midwest’s largest metropolitan areas , such as Chicago, Illinois, and Detroit, Michigan, stand out as some of the brightest features. Mid-sized cities—including Indianapolis, Indiana; Cincinnati, Ohio; and Louisville, Kentucky—and their interconnections along state and interstate highways also shine brightly.

Above the web of nighttime lights and Earth’s lower atmosphere, a diffuse layer of green and orange is visible along the horizon to the left. This band of light is airglow , produced when sunlight strikes atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere and causes them to eject photons . To the right, light from the Sun arcs across the horizon; sunrise was about an hour away on the East Coast and about two hours away in Chicago.

Astronaut photos and other remote sensing observations of nighttime lights are scientifically valuable for tracking changes in the built environment. For example, Chicago’s lightscape appears a homogeneous pale yellow in the wide view above. But in detailed photos, like the one below, a range of colors stemming from different types of lighting is discernible. Using NASA’s extensive Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth archive, researchers have developed a method for distinguishing lighting types within the pixels of nighttime photos. Systematically quantifying urban lights’ brightness, color, and extent can provide insight into how cities grow and evolve .

Satellite sensors also observe changes to lighting. In particular, NASA’s Black Marble nighttime lights product suite uses satellite observations to produce science-quality records of nighttime lights across the globe at daily, monthly, and yearly time scales. In the eastern U. S. , scientists have used these data to track everything from power outages and restoration following major storms to lighting changes associated with new infrastructure to transitions to LED lighting from older forms.

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-226709 was acquired on October 18, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters, and photograph ISS070-E-105097 was acquired on March 1, 2024, with a Nikon D5 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. They are provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The images were taken by members of the Expedition 75 and Expedition 70 crews, respectively. The images have been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed.

The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth .

For example, Chicago’s lightscape appears a homogeneous pale yellow in the wide view above. But in detailed photos, like the one below, a range of colors stemming from different types of lighting is discernible. Using NASA’s extensive Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth archive, researchers have developed a method for distinguishing lighting types within the pixels of nighttime photos. Systematically quantifying urban lights’ brightness, color, and extent can provide insight into how cities grow and evolve .

Satellite sensors also observe changes to lighting. In particular, NASA’s Black Marble nighttime lights product suite uses satellite observations to produce science-quality records of nighttime lights across the globe at daily, monthly, and yearly time scales. In the eastern U. S. , scientists have used these data to track everything from power outages and restoration following major storms to lighting changes associated with new infrastructure to transitions to LED lighting from older forms.

Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-226709 was acquired on October 18, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 14 millimeters, and photograph ISS070-E-105097 was acquired on March 1, 2024, with a Nikon D5 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. They are provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center. The images were taken by members of the Expedition 75 and Expedition 70 crews, respectively. The images have been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed.

The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the internet. Additional images taken by astronauts and cosmonauts can be viewed at the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth .

articles.title: NASA Astronaut, STEM Creator Connect with Students for STEM Day
articles.dek: Students across the country will have the opportunity to connect directly with the International Space Station during a live, interactive in-flight call with NASA astronaut…
paragraphs: Students across the country will have the opportunity to connect directly with the International Space Station during a live, interactive in-flight call with NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Mark Rober STEM content creator and founder of ClassCrunchLabs Foundation. The event, hosted by NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement, celebrates National STEM Day by bringing real‑world science, engineering, and exploration into classrooms nationwide.
The Earth-to-space call will begin at 11 a. m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 4, and will be available to watch on the agency’s flagship YouTube with additional engagement across Learn With NASA channels.

From aboard the space station, Menon will answer questions from students about living and working in microgravity, the path to becoming an astronaut, and the technologies that make human spaceflight possible. Rober, joining from California, will share how curiosity, creativity, and hands‑on problem‑solving shaped his career from NASA engineer to STEM creator.

During the downlink, students will see the space station in real time as Menon demonstrates how everyday activities, from eating to experimenting, change in microgravity. The downlink supports NASA’s broader effort to connect students with authentic STEM experiences to help build technical skills and introduce aerospace careers to students. National STEM Day is an opportunity to recognize the power of hands‑on learning and to inspire the next generation of scientists, technicians, engineers, and innovators who will carry NASA’s exploration goals forward.

This downlink also marks the launch of a new collaboration between NASA and the ClassCrunchLabs Foundation. Together, the organizations will work to broaden access to STEM learning experiences for students across the country by aligning NASA’s mission‑driven educational resources with CrunchLabs’ hands‑on engineering content. Through shared programming and outreach, the partnership aims to inspire more learners to engage with science, engineering, and problem‑solving skills that prepare them for future opportunities in the aerospace sector and beyond.
Educators and families are encouraged to tune in and celebrate National STEM Day with an inspiring conversation between a NASA astronaut in orbit and a STEM educator on Earth.
